extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners (and practitioners) on how to evaluate, admit, weigh, and respond to objective (secondary) evidence of nonobviousness (e.g., commercial success, unexpected results, criticality, failure of others) submitted in affidavits/declarations and other evidence traversing rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence must be considered when timely present
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations, when timely presented, containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered by the examiner in determining the issue of obviousness of claims for patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court holdings (e.g., Stratoflex) require consideration of secondary considerations en route to determination of obviousness; such evidence may give context to circumstances surrounding the origin of the subject matter sought to be patented and may be relevant as indicia of obviousness or unobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness requirement for evidence traversing rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections must be timely or seasonably filed to be entered and entitled to consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely categories include: (1) prior to a final rejection; (2) before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; (3) after final rejection but before or on the same date of filing an appeal upon showing good and sufficient reasons why necessary and not earlier presented; (4) after prosecution is closed if filed with a request for continued examination (RCE) or with a continued prosecution application (CPA) as appropriate. See 37 CFR and MPEP cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must consider and comment on entered evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections, when timely presented, must be considered by the examiner whenever present and all entered affidavits, declarations, and other evidence traversing rejections are acknowledged and commented upon by the examiner in the next succeeding action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extent of commentary depends on the action taken. If the evidence is sufficient to overcome the prima facie case, comments should be consistent with guidelines for statements of reasons for allowance (MPEP §1302.14). If insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why the evidence is insufficient and identify reasons in the next Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must specifically explain why evidence is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 is insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why the evidence is insufficient; general statements such as 'the declaration lacks technical validity' or 'the evidence is not commensurate with the scope of the claims' without supporting explanation are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph as a conclusion to the explanation of insufficiency and precede it by appropriate form paragraph(s) (e.g., form paragraph 7.66). Provide detailed reasons (e.g., data not convincing, lack of nexus, commercial success not related to technology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for secondary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To be of probative value, any secondary evidence must be related to the claimed invention (nexus required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'nexus' designates a factually and legally sufficient connection between the objective evidence of nonobviousness and the claimed invention so that the evidence is probative. The weight attached depends on relevance and amount/nature of the evidence. Examiner must determine whether a nexus exists between the merits of the claimed invention and the secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence should be supported by actual proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence which must be factually supported by an appropriate affidavit or declaration to be of probative value includes evidence of unexpected results, commercial success, solution of a long-felt need, inoperability of the prior art, invention before the date of the reference, and allegations that authors of the prior art derived the disclosed subject matter from the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (In re De Blauwe): unexpected results must be established by factual evidence; absence of comparative tests means assertions of unexpected results are mere argument. Provide tests/comparisons as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney arguments cannot substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The arguments of counsel cannot take the place of evidence in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney statements (e.g., asserting results, commercial success, solution of long-felt need, inoperability, invention before a reference, derivation allegations) are not evidence and must be supported by appropriate affidavits/declarations or factual record. See MPEP §2145 for case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion evidence: factual basis and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Although factual evidence is preferable, opinion testimony is entitled to consideration and some weight so long as the opinion is not on the ultimate legal conclusion at issue; an opinion as to a legal conclusion is not entitled to any weight, but the underlying basis may be persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing probative value of expert opinion, consider nature of matter sought to be established, strength of opposing evidence, interest of expert in outcome, and presence/absence of factual support. Factually-based expert opinions may rebut prima facie cases; conclusory or unsupported opinions have little value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusory affidavits generally carry little weight
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration which states only conclusions may have some probative value but may have little weight when considered in light of all the evidence of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide factual support rather than mere conclusions. Case law (e.g., Brandstadter) shows conclusory statements often insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of applicant vs. disinterested person
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit of an applicant as to the advantages of his or her claimed invention, while less persuasive than that of a disinterested person, cannot be disregarded for this reason alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant affidavits should be considered, but examiners should weigh potential bias and factual support; see Ex parte Keyes and In re McKenna for precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing objective evidence against prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: In making a final determination of patentability, evidence supporting patentability must be weighed against evidence supporting the prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ultimate determination is based on consideration of the entire record by a preponderance of evidence, giving due consideration to persuasiveness of arguments and secondary evidence. Evaluate rebuttal facts along with the facts on which the prima facie case was reached, not against the prima facie conclusion itself. Consider all competent rebuttal evidence as a whole against the evidence supporting the prima facie case (In re Piasecki).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to provide rebuttal evidence when prima facie case established
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a prima facie case of obviousness is established, the failure to provide rebuttal evidence is dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant does not present timely rebuttal evidence and prima facie case stands, rejection may be sustained. Absence of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of obviousness (Miles Labs v. Shandon).

rubrics_metrics.name: If examiner remains unconvinced, state reasons in next action
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after evaluating the evidence, the examiner is still not convinced that the claimed invention is patentable, the next Office action should include a statement to that effect and identify the reason(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific insufficiencies (e.g., commercial success not convincing; commercial success not related to the technology) and cite applicable case law (e.g., Demaco). See MPEP §2145 for guidance on sufficiency of rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected-results standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue is whether properties differ to such an extent that the difference is really unexpected (difference in kind rather than degree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., In re Waymouth) interprets 'unexpected' as marked improvement over other ratios or conditions; differences merely of degree may be insufficient. Examine the nature and significance of the difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater-than-expected results as evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater than expected result is an evidentiary factor pertinent to the legal conclusion of obviousness (or nonobviousness) of the claims at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater-than-additive (synergistic) effects may be persuasive but still must be shown to be greater than those expected from prior art and of significant, practical advantage. Examples: In re Corkill; Merck v. Biocraft; NutraSweet decisions discuss limits where prior art expected additive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of a shared property as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unobvious or unexpected advantageous properties, such as superiority in a property the claimed compound shares with the prior art, can rebut prima facie obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No set number of examples required. Demonstrate superiority in relevant tests (see In re Chupp and related Board decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an unexpected property is evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a property not possessed by the prior art is evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide factual evidence showing the property not present in prior art (e.g., In re Papesch). Unexpected properties can rebut obviousness but do not automatically mandate nonobviousness (see In re Payne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of an expected property is evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of a property which a claimed invention would have been expected to possess based on prior art teachings is evidence of unobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that prior art would have expected a property and that the claimed invention lacks it (e.g., Ex parte Mead Johnson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicant to establish unexpectedness and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Burden is on applicant to establish that the differences in results are in fact unexpected and unobvious and of both statistical and practical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere assertions or conclusions are insufficient; provide statistically and practically significant data and explain its relevance (e.g., Ex parte Gelles, Ex parte C). See In re Nolan and In re Eli Lilly for precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants must explain proffered data
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants have the burden of explaining the data in any declaration or other evidence they proffer in support of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure declarations explain methodology, comparative basis, and relevance; unsupported data or unexplained results will carry little weight (Ex parte Ishizaka).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and indirect comparative tests are probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected properties may be in the form of a direct or indirect comparison of the claimed invention with the closest prior art which is commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative testing (direct/indirect) is persuasive when scope is commensurate. For intermediates, show 'contributing cause' of end-product behavior and establish nexus between intermediate and end product (In re Magerlein). See In re Boesch, Blondel, Fouche for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh expected and unexpected properties together
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results must be weighed against evidence supporting prima facie obviousness in making a final determination of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unexpected properties are not shown to have significance equal to or greater than expected properties, they may be insufficient to rebut obviousness (In re Nolan, In re Eli Lilly). Expected beneficial results themselves are evidence of obviousness (In re Gershon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support; the showing of unexpected results must be reviewed to see if the results occur over the entire claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests limited to a narrow species may not support a broad genus unless trends allow reasonable extension. Provide sufficient tests inside and outside claimed ranges to demonstrate criticality (In re Clemens, In re Peterson, In re Grasselli, In re Kollman, In re Lindner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with the closest prior art is required
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed invention with the disclosure of each cited reference to determine the closest single prior art reference (In re Merchant). Explain deviations from reference disclosure; when testing less than all cited compounds, tests must permit a conclusion respecting relative effectiveness (In re Johnson, In re Payne). When two equally close references exist, showing unexpected results over one will not rebut unless teachings are sufficiently similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed invention may be compared with closer prior art than examiner used
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may compare the claimed invention with prior art that is more closely related to the invention than the prior art relied upon by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the most relevant prior art for comparisons where appropriate (In re Holladay, Ex parte Humber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating criticality of a claimed range requires sufficient testing
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish unexpected results over a claimed range, applicants should compare a sufficient number of tests both inside and outside the claimed range to show the criticality of the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tests across the claimed range and adjacent regions to show trends and criticality (In re Hill, In re Saunders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration/affidavit form required for assurances
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations or affidavits are required to obtain assurances that statements or representations are correct as provided by 35 U.S.C. 25 and 18 U.S.C. 1001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications may be evidence of facts and considered to the extent probative but cannot substitute for declaration/expert testimony that carries statutory assurances (Ex parte Gray). See MPEP for form requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must have nexus to claimed invention; consider totality of record
rubrics_metrics.description: Nexus between the claimed invention and evidence of commercial success is required. The totality of the record must be considered when determining whether a claimed invention would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence/arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded; commercial success unconnected to the claimed technology is not probative. Consider all give-and-take of ex parte prosecution (In re Chu, In re Zenitz, Ex parte Sasajima).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The lack of objective evidence of nonobviousness does not weigh in favor of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of secondary considerations is neutral; do not treat lack of such evidence as affirmative evidence of obviousness (Miles Labs. Inc. v. Shandon Inc.).
